extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, humorists, literary critics, and students/theorists of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical guidance for creating comic effects and comic types in drama and other arts, focusing on what makes something laughable and how to construct reproducible comic characters and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy aims at the general
rubrics_metrics.description: ONLY one of all the arts that aims at the general; so that once this objective has been attributed to it, we have said all that it is and all that the rest cannot be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy depicts characters we have already come across and shall meet again; it takes note of similarities and places types before our eyes (creates new types if necessary). This contrasts with other arts (especially tragedy) which aim at individuality. Examples: titles like Le Misanthrope, l'Avare denote whole classes; comic poets group characters as satellites to show a type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art aims to reveal reality by disinterested perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Art's loftiest ambition consists in revealing to us nature by brushing aside utilitarian symbols and conventional generalities so that we are brought face to face with reality itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art (painting, sculpture, poetry, music) reveals individualized reality by lifting the veil of practical simplifications; this purity of perception implies a break with utilitarian convention and a disinterestedness of sense or consciousness (what is called idealism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (and tragedy) aims at individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Art always aims at what is INDIVIDUAL. What the artist fixes on his canvas is something he has seen at a certain spot, on a certain day… The dramatist unfolds the life-history of a soul, something which has once happened and can never be repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic characters are unique and not meant to be grouped as repeatable types; universality in tragedy lies in the effect produced (acceptance by everybody), not in the character being a general type. Poetic imagination is inner observation—making the poet's potential selves visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characters should be types (reproducible) rather than unique individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy depicts characters we have already come across and shall meet with again. It aims at placing types before our eyes and even creates new types if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic tactic: show several different copies of the same model (satellites around the central character) to define a 'species' as the naturalist does. Many comedies have plural or collective titles (Les Femmes savantes) reflecting this orientation. Type-creation aids general laughter and social correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic observation is external, comparative, and generalising
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's observation is directed outwards; it is settling on the surface, skin-deep, dealing with persons at the point at which they come into contact and become capable of resembling one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method parallels inductive sciences: bring together scattered data, compare analogous cases, extract essence, and form categories. Comic observation avoids deep inner causes and instead abstracts repeatable features that can be generalized into types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughable traits must be unconscious/invisible to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Invisible to its actual owner, for the comic ever partakes of the unconscious; it must be visible to everybody else so that it may call forth general laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we are never ridiculous except in some point hidden from our own consciousness, comic qualities must be those the subject does not perceive; this makes the trait observable from without and amenable to correction through laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait: simultaneously deep-rooted and superficial
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be deep-rooted, so as to supply comedy with inexhaustible matter, and yet superficial, in order that it may remain within the scope of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful comic trait endures (deep-rooted) but remains observable on the surface (superficial) so the comic effect is maintainable and repeatable rather than tragic or pathological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait: considerate to self but troublesome to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely considerate to its own self, so that it may be displayed without scruple, but troublesome to others, so that they may repress it without pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This polarity makes the trait socially effective: the subject feels no shame but others are bothered, which fuels the socially corrective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait: immediately repressible yet likely to reappear
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately repressible, so that our laughter may not have been wasted, but sure of reappearing under fresh aspects, so that laughter may always find something to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trait must be fixable by a social or comic correction in the moment, yet capable of recurring so laughter remains useful and the comic material renewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait: inseparable from social life but insufferable to society
rubrics_metrics.description: Inseparable from social life, although insufferable to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits are rooted in social environments (professions, roles) so comedy can both display and correct social rigidity without attacking social life itself; laughter aims to adapt the individual back to the social whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait: versatile—attachable to vices and virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Capable—in order that it may assume the greatest imaginable variety of forms—of being tacked on to all the vices and even to a good many virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can exploit many aspects of character; even good qualities can be rendered laughable when manifested in a particular, reproducible way (e.g., vanity masked as virtue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as the central comic element
rubrics_metrics.description: This mixture is vanity. Probably there is not a single failing that is more superficial or more deep-rooted. The wounds it receives are never very serious, and yet they are seldom healed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanity underlies many laughable traits; it is 'scarcely a vice' yet draws in other vices as means to satisfy it. Laughter functions as a remedy for vanity—restoring self-consciousness and promoting sociability—so locating and exploiting vanity yields powerful comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional comic: use profession-based categories
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ready-made categories established by society itself (various trades, public services and professions) which impart habitual peculiarities to their members—small societies within Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can mine professions for reliable, reproducible comic types because professional habits produce shared traits; this yields predictable varieties of the 'professional comic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional vanity / solemnity
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional vanity: each practitioner exalts his own art above all the rest. Vanity tends to merge into SOLEMNITY in proportion to the degree of quackery in the profession under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more doubtful or questionable a profession's utility, the more practitioners treat it like a priesthood; holding this up to ridicule (e.g., Moliere's doctors) produces comic effects based on the pretentiousness and solemn language of the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional callousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic character is so tightly jammed into the rigid frame of his functions that he has no room to move or to be moved like other men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting characters who respond to human situations with professional indifference (e.g., 'Bah! cela fait toujours passer une heure ou deux') creates a coarse but effective comic contrast between human feeling and professional routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional jargon/register for ludicrous effect
rubrics_metrics.description: To confine a profession, so to say, within the four corners of its own particular jargon—applying the language of law, medicine and strategy to everyday affairs as though practitioners had become incapable of talking like ordinary people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating non-professional experience into the professional register (or vice versa) produces comic incongruity; refinement occurs when jargon reveals a deeper personal peculiarity beyond mere technical speech (examples: Regnard's Joueur, Moliere's Femmes savantes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional logic: particular ways of reasoning create comic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ways of reasoning are customary in certain circles, valid for those circles but untrue for the rest of the public; the contrast between particular logic and universal logic produces comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the gap between a group's internal reasoning and common-sense reasoning to create situations where conclusions make sense within the profession but appear absurd or laughable to outsiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy contains a specific kind of absurdity: inversion of common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is a very special inversion of common sense: seeking to mould things on an idea of one's own, instead of moulding one's ideas on things—in seeing before us what we are thinking of, instead of thinking of what we see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all absurdity is comic; the laughable arises when a privileged idea in a character's mind forces a mismatch between perception and reality (e.g., Don Quixote seeing giants where we see windmills). This 'inversion' is the comic's characteristic absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality in comedy lies in the effect produced, not the cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality here lies in the effect produced, and not in the cause. The greater the work and the more profound the truth, the more universal will that effect tend to become.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comic work's genuineness is measured by its power to compel imitation of the perception it presents; a unique portrayal can still be universally accepted if it forces the audience to make the same perceptual effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter's social function: corrective and adaptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter performs one of its main functions—that of bringing back to complete self-consciousness a certain self-admiration which is almost automatic, and thus obtaining the greatest possible sociability of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter neutralises individual 'poisons' like vanity, represses separatist rigidity, converts rigidity into plasticity, and readapts the individual to the social whole; comic art therefore has an implicitly instructive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid penetrating too deeply into personality for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: To penetrate too far into the personality, to couple the outer effect with causes that are too deep-seated, would mean to endanger and in the end to sacrifice all that was laughable in the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep causes localized in an intermediate region of the soul (not too deep) so the effect appears average and reproduces across people; delving into deep causes risks transforming comic material into tragedy or pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for creating comic types: abstraction and comparison (inductive technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the physicist's method, bringing together scattered data, comparing analogous cases and extracting their essence to obtain an average—the comic character emerges by generalisation and abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To build a comic type, observe many similar instances, isolate the recurring feature, and present it in concentrated form; this yields a reproducible, class-like comic figure rather than a mere individual portrait.
